t: Minimum Edge Toggles on a Tree — Leaf-Pruning over GF(2)
o: Each operation flips the two endpoints of one edge, so we need a subset of edges whose incidence parity matches the per-node difference start[x] != target[x]. Walk through Example 2: differences are at nodes 2, 5(? nodes where strings differ) — toggling edges 1, 2, 5 flips exactly those nodes an odd number of times. Example 3 shows the parity obstruction: every operation flips two nodes, so the total number of differing positions must be even; '00'->'01' has one difference, hence -1. With n up to 1e5 we need a linear-time constructive method rather than searching subsets.
k: The answer subset is unique on a tree: edge (parent,child) must be toggled iff the child's required parity is 1 after its subtree is resolved.
Feasible iff the number of positions where start and target differ is even.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over edge subsets
a.i: Try every subset of the n-1 edges, apply the toggles, and keep the smallest valid subset. This directly mirrors the definition and is fine only for tiny n.
s: For each subset compute the parity each node is flipped.
Accept subsets matching the target; track the minimum-size one.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — exponential; only usable for very small n.

a.i: Process the tree from the leaves inward. A leaf x has no other edges to fix its color, so its parent edge must be toggled exactly when x still needs a flip; toggling propagates the parity to the parent. This resolves every edge uniquely and yields the minimum (indeed the only) solution.
s: If the count of differing positions is odd, return [-1].
Repeatedly remove leaves: for leaf x with pending parity p, if p = 1 record its parent edge and flip the parent's parity.
Continue until all nodes are removed; the last node's parity is guaranteed 0 by the even-total check.
Sort recorded edge indices and return.
a.t: O(n log n) — linear pruning plus a final sort of the answer.
a.sp: O(n) for adjacency, degree, and parity arrays.

w: In an interview, lead with the parity observation (total differences must be even), then derive the unique leaf-pruning construction — it doubles as a proof that the minimum-length answer is unique. Pitfalls: forgetting the global parity check, mishandling the last remaining node, and forgetting to sort the output. Follow-ups: what if the graph has cycles (system may have multiple/parametrized solutions, leading to Gaussian elimination over GF(2)), or if toggling an edge had a cost (weighted version).
